(a) Fiscal Year 2007.—The Secretary of the Air Force may not retire any U–2 aircraft of the Air Force in fiscal year 2007. 
    (b) Years After Fiscal Year 2007.—
        (1) Certification required.—After fiscal year 2007, the Secretary of the Air Force may retire a U–2 aircraft only if the Secretary of Defense certifies to Congress that the intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) capabilities provided by the U–2 aircraft no longer contribute to mitigating any gaps in intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance capabilities identified in the 2006 Quadrennial Defense Review. 
        (2) Limitations.—No action may be taken by the Department of Defense to retire (or to prepare to retire) any U–2 aircraft before a certification specified in paragraph (1) is submitted to Congress. If such a certification is submitted, no such action may be taken until after the end of the 60-day period beginning on the date on which the certification is submitted.

fable.w: The tempting reading is that the certification requirement and 60-day waiting period are a procedural check before a federal decision, which resembles participation. That reading fails because the certification goes only to Congress, which is inside the federal government, and the only other actors are the Secretary of the Air Force and the Secretary of Defense. No state, tribe, company, expert, or member of the public is consulted or given a right to object or sue.
fable.s: the Secretary of the Air Force may retire a U–2 aircraft only if the Secretary of Defense certifies to Congress

opus.w: Before a U-2 can be retired, the Secretary of Defense must certify to Congress and then wait 60 days. Congress and the Department of Defense are both inside the federal government. The waiting period looks procedural, but it is a notice to Congress, not a comment period or consultation with anyone outside the government, so the definition of participation is not met.
opus.s: the Secretary of the Air Force may retire a U–2 aircraft only if the Secretary of Defense certifies to Congress
opus.b: The tempting reading is that the 60-day certification and waiting period is a procedural step before a decision, so it might count as participation. It doesn't hold up. The certification goes from the Secretary of Defense to Congress, and both are inside the federal government. No state, expert, company, or member of the public takes part in the decision to retire the aircraft.

qwen_chat.w: The section requires the Secretary of Defense to certify a finding to Congress. Since Congress is part of the federal government, this interaction is internal to the government and does not involve any outside parties such as states, tribes, or the public. The definition explicitly states that reports to Congress are not participation.
qwen_chat.s: the Secretary of Defense certifies to Congress that the intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) capabilities provided by the U–2 aircraft no longer contribute to mitigating any gaps in intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance capabilities identified in the 2006 Quadrennial Defense Review.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that the requirement for the Secretary of Defense to certify to Congress involves "participation" because it requires a formal report to an external body. However, Congress is explicitly defined as being INSIDE the federal government. Therefore, reporting to or certifying to Congress is intra-governmental communication, not participation with outside parties. The decision-making process described (whether to retire aircraft) involves only federal officials (Secretary of the Air Force, Secretary of Defense) and federal bodies (Congress). There is no consultation with states, tribes, the public, or private entities.
